newsitem.title: HONG KONG: U.S. calls shots on HK, Britain kowtows to reality.
newsitem.headline: U.S. calls shots on HK, Britain kowtows to reality.

text.p: The United States and Britain, outraging Hong Kong's pro-democracy camp, have put business first and bowed to the reality of an unelected pro-Beijing legislature.
That was how analysts on Thursday summed up the dramatic U-turn in American and British posture towards the unelected legislature that China plans to install in Hong Kong next week.

With Beijing due to dissolve the elected Legislative Council on taking back the British colony next Monday midnight, the two western powers had planned to boycott the swearing-in ceremony for the new body set for the early hours of Tuesday.

But they drew in their horns this week and diluted their opposition, with Washington deciding to send along Hong Kong Consul General Richard Boucher and London sending its two top Hong Kong diplomats, Francis Cornish and Hugh Davies.
Pro-democracy campaigners denounced the volte-face and blasted Washington and London with charges of contemptible behaviour and crass hypocrisy.
The flip-flop has left Britain's boycott policy in tatters and feisty Hong Kong Governor Chris Patten's tough pro-democracy campaign against China in shreds, political analysts said.
"Britain is belly up," said an analyst close to the government. "It's almost a kowtow."
"We're witnessing the end of British confrontation with China," analyst Sonny Lo at Hong Kong University's politics department told Reuters.
"The British decision was affected by the U.S. move. American policy supports democracy in Hong Kong but also reflects the dilemma of how to deal with the future government," Lo said.
"Strategically, the British now have to follow the American position, and this has implications for British policy on Hong Kong in the long term."

Hong Kong University's Raymond Wacks, a legal theorist and human rights law expert, likened the Anglo-American turnabout on the provisional legislature to the U.S. handling earlier this week of China's "most favoured nation" (MFN) trade status.
Washington renewed MFN for China on Tuesday in the face of vigorous opposition from a large segment of the U.S. political establishment keen to punish China for human rights abuses.
"I think it's yet another instance of economic policy dictating national policy," Wacks told Reuters.
"They perceive they might lose out in this vast market that is China. This seems to be the driving factor. They don't want to antagonise China and endanger commercial relationships."
China has often punished diplomatic sparring partners by withholding lucrative trade deals or rewarded diplomatic allies by offering them huge contracts.
Professor Peter Wesley-Smith, dean of law at Hong Kong University, said Britain was "having its cake and eating it".

"Both countries are clinging to the purity of their objections to the provisional legislature and at the same time being pragmatic, so that those who have to deal with the future authorities can do so," Wesley-Smith told Reuters.
"But neither is making concession on the legitimacy of the legislature," said Wesley-Smith, author of a soon-to-be-updated authoritative work on Hong Kong's legal history, "Unequal Treaty".

But Wacks said he believed Hong Kong democrats would mount serious court challenges to the provisional legislature over its constitutionality after the handover, and that the court of final appeal might find the body unlawful and unconstitutional.
"This has all the makings of a constitutional crisis," Wacks said, expressing a view at odds with the widely held opinion that the interim body will survive until new elections are held.
Other analysts said there were signs the British Foreign Office was at war with the government and Labour Prime Minister Tony Blair had bowed to reality after talks with U.S. President Bill Clinton.
"There has been a history of clashes between the Foreign Office diplomats and the government since Chris Patten became Hong Kong's Governor five years ago," a western diplomat said.
Blair, just a month in office, wants a brighter relationship with China after years of Sino-British bickering.
